Paper: Li et al. (2026), ball-milled/N-doped biochar for tetracycline
Issue class: Abstract-to-main-text pore-volume discrepancy and loss of adsorption performance on regeneration
Specific unresolved issue: Original ACS Omega PDF visually confirms the abstract reports QN7.5BC total pore volume = 276 cm³/g, whereas detailed characterization in the main text (PDF p.5) reports 0.2951 cm³/g and micropore volume 0.03822 cm³/g; after TC adsorption, the main text reports total pore volume 0.2532 cm³/g and micropore volume 0.01082 cm³/g. The abstract value is about 935 times the detailed main-text value and is physically implausible as a specific pore volume, but no correction/erratum is provided in the inspected source. Regeneration results state TC removal falls from 95.6% in cycle 1 to 54.6% in cycle 2 and 40.6% by cycle 6. Methods say regeneration was repeated for five consecutive cycles; this plausibly means five reuse cycles after the initial cycle and should not be labelled a separate cycle-count contradiction.
Why it matters: The abstract pore-volume claim would materially distort structural-performance comparisons if repeated. The six-cycle decline undermines claims of robust long-term reuse and sustainable cost effectiveness despite strong first-cycle removal.
Next action: Retain 0.2951 cm³/g as the detailed main-text value only with the abstract discrepancy stated; do not silently replace the published abstract. Preserve the cycle-specific decline. Verify supporting Figure S8 if exact intermediate cycle values are required; do not infer a correction for the pore-volume typo.
Resolution route: Original full PDF and rendered abstract/main-text pages verified; official ACS SI page is indexed but direct PDF retrieval was blocked in this pass.
Manuscript treatment until resolved: Do not cite 276 cm³/g. State that abstract prints 276 cm³/g but detailed characterization reports 0.2951 cm³/g; use only the latter as the detailed main-text result with explicit discrepancy. Report first-to-sixth-cycle decline as major reuse limitation; no cost/LCA claim from the word sustainable.
